The excursion takes you to Guachipas, a picturesque village in the foothills near the archaeological site of Cuevas Pintadas de Guachipas in the Las Juntas area. Among the red sandstone cliffs are more than 40 rock shelters and grottoes containing nearly a thousand rock paintings, created between 500 and 1500 CE using natural red, black, white, and yellow pigments. The panels depict caravans of llamas, anthropomorphic "shield people" (hombres escudos), and scenes of rituals and hunting. Together, they form one of the most significant collections of rock art in northwestern Argentina. The route passes through some of Salta Province's most striking landscapes, with winding mountain roads, cactus forests, and panoramic views of the Calchaquí Valley.

Depart for one of Latin America's most important religious centers, the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Guadalupe, where Holy Mass will be celebrated.
Visit the Old and New Basilicas, Tepeyac Hill, the Chapel of the Indians and the Chapel of the Well, the gardens, and the original tilma on which, according to tradition, the image of the Virgin Mary miraculously appeared before the young Indigenous man Juan Diego.
Continue to the National Museum of Anthropology, one of the most important museums in Mexico and the Americas. The museum preserves and displays the archaeological heritage of Mesoamerican peoples while introducing visitors to the country's contemporary ethnic diversity.

From Medellín, travel to Guatapé, where brightly colored facades are decorated with zócalos, traditional raised panels depicting scenes of local life.

The next stop is El Peñón de Guatapé, also known as La Piedra del Peñol. The monolith rises approximately 220 meters above the surrounding landscape. From the top, enjoy a sweeping panorama of the reservoir, its green shores, and numerous islands.

After visiting the rock, continue with a leisurely walk through Guatapé. Take a closer look at the decorative base panels, colorful architecture, and waterfront. At the end of the excursion, return to Medellín.

## A City Among the Amazon's Rivers

Manaus is often seen as a gateway to the jungle, yet the city itself deserves to be explored. Its architecture reflects the wealth of the rubber boom: buildings in the historic center still convey the ambitions and tastes of that era. The Amazonas Theatre has become one of the city's best-known landmarks, while the surrounding streets offer a glimpse of everyday life in the capital of Amazonas state.

River commerce, local cuisine, and Indigenous heritage are closely intertwined here. At the Adolpho Lisboa Market, you can discover regional produce, while the riverfront makes it especially clear how central water is to life in Manaus. This urban perspective on the Amazon complements the experience of its forests and jungle lodges.

A sightseeing tour is a good introduction to Manaus. The landmarks described here help you get to know the city; specific stops and interior visits depend on the agreed itinerary. Light clothing and comfortable shoes are recommended for walking.

The tour costs $190 per person.

## Corcovado and the Forest in Half a Day

Corcovado reveals the layout of Rio: city neighborhoods fill the spaces between mountains, coastline, and green slopes. At the summit stands the Christ the Redeemer statue, surrounded by sweeping panoramic views. On a clear day, your gaze can wander from the buildings to the water and back again; clouds can quickly transform the entire scene.

Tijuca Forest reveals another side of the city. Restoration began here in the 19th century, and today the forest forms part of a national park. Beneath the tree canopy, you can see just how close lush tropical vegetation lies to the urban landscape. Listen to the sounds of the forest and take in the dense greenery.

This private half-day tour combines Corcovado and Tijuca Forest. It is a convenient way to experience Rio's natural surroundings when you have only part of a day available. The way up, specific stops, and visiting arrangements are agreed upon when booking.
